title: Better luck next time: Learning through retaking
summary_en: If you didn't get the score you wanted, should you take the SAT again? Frisancho, Krishna and co-authors document who actually retakes the test and how retaking pays off. They show that retake rates are systematically lower among low-income and minority students — the very groups most likely to gain from a higher second attempt — and that policies lowering retake costs would disproportionately benefit them. The paper became a reference for the literature on how exam-system frictions widen educational inequality.
data_used: US administrative SAT-taker data with full retake histories, scores on each attempt, demographic information, and (where merged) college-enrolment outcomes. Estimation compares retakers to non-retakers within score bands and identifies retaking-cost effects.
policy_relevance: Useful for Hungarian admissions-test policy debates (felvi, érettségi reform): supports lowering retake fees and calendar restrictions for the érettségi, especially given the disproportionate cost to low-income students. Translation caveat: the SAT operates as a private, fee-charging market while the érettségi is public — but the inequality channel transfers to any high-stakes exam where retaking carries non-trivial fixed costs.
